title: Resolving to Renounce the World
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: (Master Hanshan Deqing, Mengyou ji: "Instruction to Chan Practitioner Wusheng Lu")

inline.s: The ancients, at their first awakening of resolve, truly concerned themselves with the great matter of birth and death and firmly resolved to renounce the world. They severed their affections and left their parents, sought out teachers and visited friends, and endured every hardship. In every thought and recollection they grieved only that the matter of their own selves was not yet clear; their sorrow and urgency were as of one mourning for deceased parents. The moment they saw a wise teacher, they were like an infant finding its mother. If they received even a single word or half a phrase to open and guide their minds, it was like a sick person obtaining medicine. When a single thought struck true and the mind became thoroughly awakened, it was like a poor person finding a treasure. They risked their bodies and gave up their lives, sinking into obscurity and lowly service, and never shrank from toil. Consider the Second Patriarch, who settled his mind and cut off his arm; the Sixth Patriarch, who carried stones at his waist; Baizhang, who labored personally; and Yangqi, who served the assembly. Every one recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp and radiant through the ages arose from hardship. Even the Buddhas of the past, seeking unsurpassed bodhi, gave up their bodies and lives countless as motes of dust; there was no realm of beings they did not enter, no body in which they did not practice austerities. Through a hundred kalpas of cultivating causes, they attracted, in the heavens and among humans
(here the variant character is read as "among")

, offerings without measure; and even the descendants of this final age of the Dharma still enjoy a portion of the merit within the white curl of the Buddha's brow without exhausting it. How could there ever be a Maitreya born ready-made, or a Shakyamuni arising of his own accord?!

The ancients, at their first awakening of resolve, genuinely sought to be free of the great matter of birth and death, and firmly resolved to leave the cycle of rebirth. They therefore severed their affections and left their parents to become monks, sought out teachers and visited friends in quest of the Way, and endured every hardship and difficulty. In every thought and recollection they grieved only that the great matter of their own birth and death was not yet clear; their sorrow and urgency were like mourning for their parents. The moment they saw a true spiritual friend, they were like an infant finding its mother. If they obtained even a word or half a phrase to open and guide their minds, it was like a sick person obtaining medicine. When a single thought struck true and the mind was thoroughly awakened, it was like a poor person finding a treasure. They staked body and life, and in silence and obscurity willingly undertook lowly service, never fearing toil and hardship. Consider the Second Patriarch Huike, who settled his mind and cut off his arm; the Sixth Patriarch, who wore a stone at his waist to hull rice; Baizhang, who performed labor himself; and Yangqi, who served the assembly. All who are recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp and the other histories of the Chan lineage through the ages, and who shine through the ages, arose from hardship. Even the Buddhas of the past, seeking unsurpassed bodhi, gave up their bodies and lives countless as motes of dust; there was no realm of beings in which they did not take a body, no body in which they did not practice austerities. Through a hundred kalpas of cultivating causes, they attracted offerings without measure from the heavens and among humans; and even the descendants of this final age of the Dharma are still enjoying a portion of the merit within Shakyamuni Buddha's white curl of the brow without exhausting it. How could there ever be a Maitreya born ready-made, or a Shakyamuni arising naturally of his own accord!

[like mourning for one's parents] to grieve as sorrowfully as if one's own father and mother had died. Kao means father; bi means mother. [staking body and life] to risk body and life. Here ban is the ancient form of pan, which is the same as pin. [sinking into obscurity] also written lu chen, to be buried and unknown. [never shrinking from toil] dan means to fear. [settling the mind and cutting off the arm] Huike (originally named Shenguang) had deeply studied the Tripitaka and wished to have his mind settled by Bodhidharma, and his request was most sincere. He stood all night in the snow; when dawn came he was still not admitted, so he cut off his own left arm to show the utmost sincerity of his quest for the Way, and thereupon met the Patriarch face to face and was greatly awakened. Later he received Bodhidharma's robe and bowl and continued the Chan lineage as the Second Patriarch. [Baizhang's personal labor] Chan Master Baizhang established the self-sufficient system of farming and Chan, putting forward the maxim "a day without work is a day without food," and practiced it himself, always being the first to labor at any task. The monk in charge, seeing him old yet still leading the work, could not bear it, and urged him to stop going to the fields, hiding his tools. Unable to find his tools anywhere, Baizhang refused to eat, in order to carry out the principle of "a day without work is a day without food." [Yangqi's serving the assembly] Yangqi was the founding patriarch of the Yangqi school of the Linji tradition in the Northern Song dynasty. Under the sixth-generation Linji master Ciming Yuan, he personally took up menial duties, enduring a thousand hardships and never shrinking from toil. [countless as motes of dust] a metaphor for an extremely great number. [still enjoying a portion of the merit within the white curl without exhausting it] In the Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury, the Buddha said: "There may be bhikshus who, having left home and received the precepts in my Dharma, practice diligently within this Dharma. Even if the gods and humans do not think of them, if they can only practice the Way with single-minded diligence, in the end they will not lack clothing and food. Why is this? The Tathagata's store of blessings is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Shariputra, after the Tathagata's passing, of the billions of parts of the white-curl mark, one part is offered to the relics and to the disciples. Shariputra, even if all the people of the world were to leave home together and practice in accord with the Dharma, they would not exhaust even one of the billions of parts of the white-curl mark. Shariputra, such is the Tathagata's immeasurable merit that whatever food and necessities the bhikshus receive will be just sufficient. Shariputra, these bhikshus should think in this way, and should not, for the sake of necessities, practice wrongful livelihoods and evil ways."

Bitterly reflecting on this final age of the Dharma, when the age of the Sage is already distant and the standards of the Dharma have been swept to the ground: we sons of the home-leaving life do not even know what we left home for. From birth we have known only to fear hunger and cold and to seek food and warmth. Once we enter the gate of emptiness, we cling to worldly habits, idly chatting all day, holding our bellies in laughter and giving free rein to our feelings, indulging the six sense faculties and piling up every kind of evil. We eat fine food without tilling, and wear fine clothes without raising silkworms. We waste in vain the offerings of the faithful and squander our precious time. We do not know whence birth comes or whither death goes. Still less do we know that cause and effect cannot be escaped and that retribution for good and evil is never mistaken. When the great limit suddenly arrives, it is like a stone thrown into water. The bitter suffering of the three evil paths, a single retribution of five thousand kalpas — and to lift one's head again, who knows when? To speak of this is painful and heartbreaking. And looking at the current of the times, such people are everywhere, wave upon wave. To hope for true practitioners among us is like sifting sand for gold: not to say there are none at all, but they are rare indeed.

Bitterly reflecting on this final age of the Dharma, when the age of the Sage is distant and the rules and standards of the Buddha's way have been swept to the ground: we sons of the home-leaving life do not even know for what matter we left home. From birth we have known only to fear hunger and cold and to seek food and warmth. Once we enter the gate of emptiness, we still cling to vulgar worldly habits, idly chatting all day, laughing and giving free rein to our feelings, indulging the six sense faculties and piling up every kind of evil. We eat fine food without tilling, and wear fine clothes without weaving. We waste in vain the offerings of the faithful and squander our precious time. We do not even know whence birth comes or whither death goes. Still less do we know that cause and effect cannot be escaped and that the retribution of good and evil is never mistaken. When the great limit — death — suddenly arrives, it is like a stone thrown into water, sinking straight to the bottom. The bitter suffering of the three evil paths: a single retribution of five thousand kalpas, and to lift one's head again — who knows what year or month that will be! To speak of this is painful and heartbreaking. And looking at such people, they are everywhere. To hope for true practitioners among us is like sifting sand for gold: not to say there are none at all, but they are rare indeed.

[dian xing] refers to the standards handed down. Gui Youguang, in his Colophon to the Portraits of Confucius's Seventy Disciples, says: "Though the ages are distant, the standards remain." Master Hanshan Deqing, in Mengyou ji, "Instruction to Chan Master Zhijian of Guizong," says: "Only Baizhang's 'a day without work is a day without food' has become the eternal standard of the monasteries." [sao di] to lose utterly. [yin xun] to cling to old habits. [peng fu] to hold one's belly — describing loud laughter, for example "to hold one's belly and laugh," "to make one hold one's belly." [the three evil paths] the path of blood, the path of blades, and the path of fire. The path of blood is the realm of animals, where animals are constantly being killed or devouring one another; the path of blades is the realm of hungry ghosts, where hungry ghosts are constantly afflicted by hunger or pressed by swords and staffs; the path of fire is the realm of hell, where beings are constantly tormented by freezing ice or searing flames. The "three paths" is another name for the three evil realms. [the three paths' bitter suffering, one retribution of five thousand] A verse says: "One retribution in the three evil paths lasts five thousand kalpas; when will one ever lift one's head again?"

Alas! The triple world is a prison, the four modes of birth are fetters and shackles, and the perilous house of birth and death is consumed by a great fire. How can one quench these fierce flames, leave all suffering behind, and reach the place of fearlessness? Only a great hero endowed with the root of spiritual capacity and bearing the bones of past practice can rouse fierce courage and leap straight through in a single bound. You are fortunate to have been born when the Buddhadharma is present, to wear the kasaya, to have met a wise teacher early, and to be complete in the six sense faculties. If you do not bitterly reflect on impermanence, deeply contemplate the great matter, think of the sufferings of hell, arouse the bodhi mind, reform the past and cultivate the future, practice diligently day and night, and strive early for liberation — but instead idle away your days and let body and mind run loose — then when the great limit arrives, what use will regret be? Alas, go now! Do not forget my parting words of admonition, lest you fail me and fail yourself.

Do not forget my parting words of admonition, lest you fail me and fail yourself!
[the four modes of birth] birth from a womb, birth from an egg, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation. [zhì gù] fetters and handcuffs.
